analysis.one_liner: Bars new deepwater drilling permits in the Gulf until the oil spill stopped and Congress found its cause.
analysis.headline: The bill, introduced during the Deepwater Horizon oil spill, never left committee and got no vote before the Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: A month into the Deepwater Horizon disaster, which was spilling millions of gallons of oil into the Gulf of Mexico, this bill would have stopped the federal government from issuing any new deepwater drilling permits or safety waivers in the Gulf until two things happened: the leak was stopped, and a congressional committee issued a report finding what caused the explosion. It was never acted on.
analysis.who_benefits: Gulf coast residents, fishing and tourism businesses, and coastal ecosystems would be protected from additional deepwater spills while the cause of the disaster was investigated. Workers on existing rigs would operate under rules the bill made harder to waive.

how_it_helps.text: The bill prohibited the Minerals Management Service from issuing any deepwater drilling permit or any waiver of environmental or safety requirements in the Gulf of Mexico until the Deepwater Horizon oil discharge had stopped and a congressional committee had issued a report finding the cause of the explosion [S2] [S3].
The bill applied to rigs drilling in water deeper than 1,000 feet, the category that included the rig that exploded [S3].

analysis.who_pays: Offshore oil and gas companies would be unable to obtain new deepwater drilling permits or waivers in the Gulf until the conditions were met, delaying new exploration and production.

drawbacks.text: A halt on new deepwater permits in the Gulf would delay drilling activity, which supports jobs and energy production along the Gulf coast; drillers and Gulf energy-dependent communities would bear that cost [S2] [S3].

The bill tied the moratorium to a congressional committee report finding the cause of the explosion, giving Congress itself the power to decide when drilling could resume, which critics could view as an indefinite or politically conditioned delay [S3].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The bill's protection was conditional and time-limited by design: it lifted automatically once the leak stopped and a cause was officially found, so the cost to drillers was a temporary delay rather than a permanent ban. Its main weakness was that it never moved, so neither the protection nor the delay ever took effect.

outcome.mechanism: It was sent to the House Natural Resources Committee and then to a subcommittee, and stayed there until the Congress ended, never receiving a hearing or a floor vote.

narrative.text: Rep. Vern Buchanan introduced the bill on May 27, 2010, about five weeks after the Deepwater Horizon explosion began the largest marine oil spill in U.S. history [S1] [S2].

The bill was referred the same day to the House Committee on Natural Resources, and on June 1, 2010, it was referred to that committee's Subcommittee on Energy and Mineral Resources; no further action is recorded [S5].
No member of the House cosponsored the bill [S4].
The bill received no vote in either chamber before the 111th Congress ended on January 3, 2011 [S1].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Deepwater drilling operators and oil and gas companies were better off, since no Gulf drilling permit moratorium ever took effect. Gulf coast residents and fishing and tourism businesses got no added protection from this bill, though other spill response and regulatory actions occurred outside of it.

for.name: Rep. Vern Buchanan
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill to freeze deepwater Gulf drilling permits and waivers until the spill stopped and Congress reported its cause.

against.name: House Natural Resources Committee
against.what_they_did: Received the bill by referral, routed it to the Subcommittee on Energy and Mineral Resources, and took no further action on it.

against.name: Offshore oil and gas industry
against.what_they_did: Would have faced a halt on new deepwater Gulf permits and safety waivers under the bill; its general opposition to Gulf drilling restrictions during this period is widely reported.

sides.party_line_note: The bill had a single Republican sponsor and no cosponsors of either party, so the record shows no measurable partisan alignment either way [S4].

industries.note: The bill would have frozen new deepwater drilling permits and blocked safety waivers in the Gulf of Mexico until the spill stopped and its cause was officially found. The industry's interest in continued permitting ran against the coastal protection the bill offered.
Fewer deepwater rigs operating without permit review meant less spill risk for Gulf waters that fisheries depend on. The industry's interest ran alongside coastal residents'.
The Deepwater Horizon spill damaged Gulf beaches and tourism; preventing additional spills protected the industry's revenue base and the public's coastline.
